newsitem.title: USA: Court martial trial to begin in Army rape case.
newsitem.headline: Court martial trial to begin in Army rape case.

text.p: Army prosecutors at the court-martial of a drill sergeant accused of raping six women said in opening statements on Friday the noncommissioned officer used the power of his rank to prey on female trainees.

"This case is about rape. It's about power, access, and control," Capt. David Thomas said as Sgt. Delmar Simpson's court-martial began as part of the U.S. military's biggest sex scandal since the Navy was rocked by the 1991 Tailhook affair.

Simpson's attorneys said their client had engaged only in consensual acts of sex, to which he has pleaded guilty, and said the Army used an overly aggressive investigation to coerce accusations of rape out of witnesses.

"A number of female soldiers in training were attracted to and willingly engaged in sexual intercourse with Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson," defence attorney Capt. Edward Brady said in his opening statement. He said Army investigators used a "heavy hand" in taking statements from witnesses and "aggressively and actively encouraged them to exaggerate and embellish their statements."

Simpson, 32, faces 19 counts of rape and 55 other charges of sexual misconduct and other crimes involving 22 women. The alleged acts occurred between November 1994 and August 1996, while Simpson served as a drill instructor at the Army's Ordnance Centre and School at the Aberdeen Proving Ground.

His was the highest-profile case and the first court-martial in an investigation that led to charges of sexual misconduct against 10 trainers at the proving ground. Four of the 10 cases have been resolved through plea agreements or administrative proceedings.

The investigation prompted a nationwide military probe into sexual harassment after it was disclosed in November. It has led to criticism that the military failed to prevent the sexual harassment as well as to charges that investigators unfairly targeted black soldiers and tried to coerce rape accusations from witnesses.

Simpson pleaded guilty to 16 of the counts against him -- 11 counts of improper sexual intercourse with trainees and five counts of propositioning. But he pleaded innocent to the rapes and other misconduct charges.

It was the biggest U.S. military sex scandal since the Tailhook convention of drunken naval pilots and sailors in Las Vegas turned into a vicious bacchanal in which 83 women were assaulted. The Navy is still trying to recover from that.

The Army scandal has not had such wide-ranging consequences and Simpson's lawyers say the case against their client is the result of over-zealous investigators. "When you get into rape and indecent assault, that's a whole different category than fraternisation and socializing type regulation," Simpson's civilian attorney Frank Spinner said this week.
Deciding the case, which is expected to last two to three weeks, will be a six-member military jury composed of one white woman, two black men and three white men. Four of the jurors are officers.

Simpson faces a maximum penalty of life in prison if convicted of rape. On the guilty pleas, he faces a total maximum penalty of 32 years in jail, a dishonourable discharge and forfeiture of pay and allowances.
